questions.q: Why isn't the connectivity built in Lesson 17 (a VPN tunnel or colocation meet-point) enough on its own for services to find each other?
options: It solves routing between the two networks, but it does not solve name resolution — services still can't look each other up by name
It only works for traffic initiated from AWS toward Azure, never the other direction
It automatically breaks once more than one subnet is added to either VNet or VPC
It requires both clouds to use the exact same IP address range before any traffic can flow
questions.explain: A VPN tunnel or meet-point gets packets from a VNet to a VPC, but Azure's DNS has never heard of AWS's private zones and vice versa, so name resolution is a separate problem entirely.

questions.q: Why is hardcoding a cross-cloud private IP address into configuration specifically risky?
options: Private IP addresses are not allowed to cross a VPN tunnel under any circumstances
Hardcoded IPs are always rejected by both clouds' network security groups
Those IPs typically sit behind a load balancer, NAT gateway, or autoscaling group, so they can change at the next scale event
AWS and Azure use identical private IP ranges by default, causing an immediate conflict
questions.explain: Cross-cloud private IPs usually sit behind infrastructure that can reassign them, so a hardcoded address that worked at deploy time can silently break later.

questions.q: In the cross-cloud DNS pattern described, what changes from the on-premises hybrid-DNS pattern in Lesson 11?
options: The entire Resolver inbound/outbound endpoint model is replaced by a different mechanism
The same inbound/outbound endpoint model is reused, but the 'outside' query source is now the other cloud instead of on-premises
Only Azure needs a Resolver configured; AWS resolves everything automatically
DNS forwarding rules are no longer needed because BGP handles name resolution
questions.explain: The building blocks are identical to hybrid DNS architecture — Azure's Private DNS Resolver and AWS's Route 53 Resolver — just pointed at each other across the Lesson 17 link instead of at on-premises.

questions.q: Why does this lesson configure forwarding in both directions (Azure-to-AWS and AWS-to-Azure) rather than just one?
options: Because name resolution across a cross-cloud link is not automatically bidirectional just because the network path is
Because AWS's Route 53 Resolver cannot send queries, only receive them
Because Azure's Private DNS Resolver only supports inbound endpoints, never outbound
Bidirectional forwarding is only needed when more than two clouds are involved
questions.explain: Each side's outbound endpoint and forwarding rule has to be configured independently; a working path in one direction says nothing about the other direction.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to decide which cloud's DNS zone is authoritative for a given cross-cloud internal name?
options: Run one unified zone split evenly across both clouds' native DNS services
Let whichever cloud resolves the query first become the source of truth for that query
Avoid giving any names ownership and resolve everything through static IP lists instead
Split ownership explicitly by domain, so each cloud's private zone is authoritative for its own names and a clear naming convention marks which is which
questions.explain: A workable pattern splits ownership cleanly by domain — e.g. azure.internal owned by Azure, aws.internal owned by AWS — because no single cloud's native zone can be sole source of truth for records the other cloud's control plane needs to write.
